title: The term ‘Dust Bowl’ first appeared in a news story about a single 1935 storm

cover.alt: Black-and-white film still of a bare, ploughed field with loose soil streaming across it in the wind.
cover.credit: US Resettlement Administration (Pare Lorentz) · Public domain

body: On 14 April 1935, remembered as **Black Sunday**, a cold front from Canada drove a wall of dust south across the Great Plains at about 60 mph. Associated Press reporter Robert E. Geiger saw it in Boise City, Oklahoma, and the AP’s Kansas City news editor, Edward Stanley, coined the term **Dust Bowl** while rewriting Geiger’s story. The storms were partly man-made: deep ploughing had removed the deep-rooted native grasses that held the soil, so when drought struck in the 1930s the bare topsoil dried to powder and blew away.

slides.alt: Black-and-white film of wind blowing loose soil across a bare ploughed field, past a fence post and a bush, and smoking off the crest of a soil drift.
slides.caption: Wind strips loose soil from bare, ploughed fields, in footage from The Plow That Broke the Plains, a 1936 US government film about the Dust Bowl.
slides.credit: US Resettlement Administration (Pare Lorentz) · Public domain · excerpt

slides.label: of Great Plains dust, about 5,400 tonnes, fell on Chicago in a two-day storm in May 1934
slides.text: Two days later the same storm reached Cleveland, Buffalo, Boston, New York City and Washington, D.C. That winter, red snow fell on New England.

slides.heading: How farmland turned into dust storms

steps.label: Wet years draw farmers to plough the prairie
1930s drought dries the bare soil to powder

slides.question: Between 1930 and 1940, about how many people moved out of the Plains states?
slides.explanation: About 3.5 million. Many families, often called ‘Okies’, headed for California, only to find the Great Depression had made life there little better.

slides.question: Before the farms came, what held the Plains soil in place through droughts?
slides.explanation: Native prairie grasses trapped soil and moisture even in drought and high winds. Deep ploughing removed them, leaving bare soil for the wind.
